details:
**"Vanished into the Clouds"**
A chapter of The Tale of Genji (Kumogakure) that has a title but no text. Its blankness implies the death of the protagonist, Genji, and it is the single most common clue for the novel. The chapters after it skip ahead to the next generation.

**Lady Murasaki (Murasaki Shikibu)**
The author of The Tale of Genji, a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese imperial court in the early 11th century, during the Heian period. The novel has 54 chapters and is often called the world's first novel. Her pen name comes from the novel's heroine Murasaki.

**Genji, the "Shining Prince"**
The title character, called Hikaru Genji ("the Shining Genji") because of his beauty and talent. He is the son of the Kiritsubo Emperor and a low-ranking consort, the Kiritsubo ("Paulownia Court") lady, who dies when he is three. After a Korean physiognomist warns that disorder would follow if he became emperor, he is made a commoner with the surname Minamoto (Genji).

**Lady Aoi**
Genji's first wife, the daughter of the Minister of the Left and sister of his friend To no Chujo, married to him at the end of Chapter 1. Their marriage is cold. After giving birth to their son Yugiri she is killed by the jealous spirit of Lady Rokujo.

**Lady Fujitsubo**
The Kiritsubo Emperor's consort and Genji's stepmother, chosen because she resembles Genji's dead mother. Genji has an affair with her, and she secretly bears his son, who becomes Emperor Reizei.

**The Uji chapters, Kaoru and Niou**
The final ten chapters, set mainly near the town of Uji after Genji's death. They follow the rivalry between Kaoru, the "fragrant captain," and Niou. Kaoru is legally Genji's son by the Third Princess but actually the son of Kashiwagi, and he has a natural fragrance; he is sometimes called literature's first antihero. Niou is Genji's grandson through his daughter by the Akashi Lady. The two pursue the daughters of the Eighth Prince.

**Exile to Suma and Akashi**
After Genji's affair with Oborozukiyo, the "Lady of the Misty Moon" and a concubine of his half-brother, the Suzaku Emperor, is discovered, he goes into exile at Suma. During a storm he dreams of his dead father and of the "king of the dragon palace." The Akashi Novice then invites him to Akashi along the shore, where Genji fathers a daughter with the Akashi Lady before being recalled to the capital.

**Murasaki (the young girl)**
A ten-year-old girl, Fujitsubo's niece, whom Genji takes from her home and raises to be his ideal wife. She becomes his great love and is often associated with the purple gromwell (murasaki) flower. Her death late in the novel plunges Genji into grief and leads to his withdrawal.

**Lady Rokujo's vengeful spirit and the Battle of the Carriages**
Lady Rokujo is Genji's proud, jealous former mistress. At the Kamo festival her carriage is shoved aside by Aoi's servants in the "Battle (Quarrel) of the Carriages." Afterward her living spirit possesses and kills Aoi, and spirits connected to her plague other women Genji loves.

**"Waves of the Blue Sea" (Seigaiha) dance**
At the autumn maple excursion before the court, Genji performs this dance flawlessly alongside To no Chujo. Next to him, his partner is compared to a mountain shrub beside a blossoming tree.

**Utsusemi, the "Locust/Cicada Shell"**
A married woman who rejects Genji's advances by slipping away and leaving behind a robe. In a poem he compares the robe to a cast-off cicada shell. Many women in the novel are known by such nicknames from poems or traits rather than true names.

**Yugao, the "Lady of the Evening Faces"**
A gentle lover of Genji's who dies mysteriously, apparently killed by a possessing spirit, during a night at an abandoned villa. Her body is secretly taken to the mountains, and Genji falls ill afterward. Her daughter Tamakazura later becomes his adoptive daughter.

**The Broom Tree chapter and the "rainy night" discussion**
In this early chapter, Genji, To no Chujo, and other young men rate types of women on a rainy night. A man from the Ministry of Rites describes a learned woman who wrote in Chinese and smelled of garlic medicine taken for a cold. The chapter's title refers to a poem connected with Utsusemi.

**Suetsumuhana (the "Safflower") and the Lady of the Orange Blossoms**
Suetsumuhana is a shy, impoverished princess whose zither playing attracts Genji but who turns out to have a long red nose, so her nickname puns on the red safflower. Hanachirusato, the "Lady of the Orange Blossoms," is a gentle lover whom Genji keeps under his care.

**Ukifune and "The Mayfly"**
Ukifune, the unacknowledged third daughter of the Eighth Prince, is torn between Kaoru and Niou and tries to drown herself in the Uji River. She is rescued and becomes a nun, which is the novel's final major event.

**Other notable scenes and context**
Genji releases fireflies to reveal his adoptive daughter Tamakazura to a suitor, and he builds a mansion, the Rokujo-in, with quarters for the four seasons to house his main lovers. He wins a picture contest using paintings he made in exile at Suma. Key ideas and context include mono no aware ("the sadness of things"), allusions to Bai Juyi's "Song of Everlasting Sorrow," the 12th-century illustrated Genji scrolls, and English translations by Arthur Waley and Royall Tyler.
